Now: In Depth!

I used to believe that chemistry was inevitable or impossible. That is to say, for any one person, when looking at another person, they were either always going to end up attracted to them or were never going to end up attracted to them. I suppose in some ways, that hasn't actually changed--but what has changed are the implications AND how to respond to these outcomes. As recently as 2012, I believed that if you become attracted to someone, you can't be friends anymore because the social pressure of unrequited romantic attachment will metaphorically but no less painfully flay you alive. This was the biggest change of all.

See, a while back, I saw this fantastic TED talk, Are Humans Sexual Omnivores? by Christopher Ryan. This happened to correspond with a friend trying to explain to me that she was romantically interested in me but didn't believe in relationship exclusivity and wanted me to neither A) restrict myself to only her, nor B) expect her to restrict herself. It also happened after reading Robert A. Heinlein's "The Moon is a Harsh Mistress", wherein some extremely interesting human relationship structures were presented.

I can't say exactly when it happened, but at some point it got through my skull that:

  1. Attraction is not a choice. It just happens.
  2. How I respond to that attraction is a choice.
  3. I have to be honest. I absolutely must disclose if I start to feel romantically attached to someone if it doesn't go away after a while.
  4. Once I admit it, I actually don't have to "get all weird" about it. That's the thing. That right there.

What do you do to enact part 4? It's kind of a doozie, and more of a 'practice makes perfect' thing. I fear that reading about it won't help very much on its own...

What it comes down to is empathy, and empiricism. These are two opposite ends of a spectrum here, one being hyper-subjectivity, the other being the very essence of objectivity. You WILL encounter cognitive dissonance until you know the layout. Because what you have to do is try to put yourself into the perspective of the person you're feeling attracted toward, and then ruthlessly hack away at the model you've constructed of them in your mind, attempting to scour away as many preconceived notions as possible--specifically striving to seek and destroy any element you wish were true AS WELL as any element you are afraid is true.

Once you have purged this mental model of the object of your desires of as much personal bias as possible through pure rote observational rigor, you can more accurately simulate what the outcomes of your actions might reasonably be. Or, to put a finer point on it, you prove to yourself how much happier you and everyone around you will be if you stop actively trying to get into their pants.

Because, believe it or not, everyone I've been in this situation with myself (no small number!) are actually really understanding and cool with it that maybe I might act a bit weird sometimes, because they know it's not on purpose. They know that if I'm stumbling over my own words or accidentally avoiding looking at them too much for fear of staring, it's because I'm just trying to not be rude. They know I'm doing my best, and hell, that's more than they can expect from most people, really!

I also learned this: Love, at its very core, is unconditional. If it's conditional, then I'm sorry but it's just not love. We're taught that it is, but it's really toxic and hurts a lot of people!

THINGS LOVE IS NOT:

  • A weapon
  • A tool
  • A currency

Most of the pain we suffer in relationships stems from attempting to treat it as such.
Withholding it unless conditions are met, as if someone must buy it--or bending over backwards for someone else to 'earn' it--treats it like a currency, and all this ever does is cheapen it, damage it, and shorten its lifespan.
Justifying acts of cruelty with love, 'crimes of passion', jealousy and envy, revenge and abuse of very many shades are all examples of love being used as a weapon.
Casting doubt on someone's love, "If you loved me you would...", or otherwise attempting to manipulate a person through their love of you--or even manipulating YOURSELF to grand gestures of martyrdom for the sake of 'love', is treating it like a tool.

Deep down at its most basic level, Love is simply a correlation of well being. When you want someone to feel safe, comfortable, and happy, you love them. And I mean actually WANT, not just the mere acknowledgement that it would be nice, or that ethically it sounds correct. It has a proven evolutionary basis, in that exercising countless computer models of the Prisoner's Dilemma we've conclusively found that cooperation reaps disproportionately higher rewards than competition simply due to how probability works in our universe. The chemical reactions responsible for the feeling we call 'love' only exist to perpetuate these wildly successful population-wide survival behaviors.

The reason I get into this here is because, if you understand what the underlying mechanism is, you can fulfill it without turning gross or pervy. You can separate what we call classical "Romantic Love" into its components and satisfy them separately. Romantic Love as we know it is actually the base foundation of unconditional love, plus physical chemistry, plus intellectual fascination. Every friendship you've ever had that deserves to be called a friendship already consists of unconditional love. Without unconditional love, physical chemistry and intellectual fascination are pure lust, which results in little more than intense but brief affairs. Unconditional Love and Fascination without Chemistry are what folks tend to call 'puppy love', where as soon as the fascination wears off (it always comes and goes) the whole thing will either (disastrously) disintegrate entirely or (hopefully) just revert back to unconditional love/friendship. Lastly, Love and Chemistry can rarely turn into "friends with benefits", but that requires both parties being open minded enough, self-aware enough, and understanding enough of what they're getting into before it can happen. Your initial question, OP, isn't whether a relationship is natural, but whether Chemistry and Fascination are, themselves.

And they aren't always. Often times they're one-sided, which hurts, but acknowledging it can at least alleviate it and the core principle of the unconditional component can survive, allowing the friendship to resume after the turbulence passes.

I myself, when I fall in love with someone, I never seem to fall 'out of' love with them. And I'm coming to accept that on the unconditional level I can love pretty much anybody/everybody. But if they aren't feeling any chemistry in return, that's fine... because, I have others upon whom I can depend. Since I've accepted that it doesn't have to be exclusive, I have three people I can go to for comfort and support while I 'get it out of my system' and acclimate to the attraction being there. Then I can just channel it all into just being helpful. The trick to it not being creepy is knowing what the creepy stuff is and redirecting it to people I trust who actually want it, and being honest about dealing with it while it's still an issue.

Accusations that he's a traitor and that she's... worse things. Fuck no. I understand that the compatibility doesn't go both ways there. They're GOOD for each other. Everybody in our entire circle feels much the same way. And I unconditionally love the both of them, and that allows me to see past my own selfish urges. Eventually all the disruptive stuff faded into the background, and we resumed hanging out like always. Hell they didn't even want me to leave last night x_x;

When I didn't know myself so well back in 2010, there was a friend I had who I had become crazy about, though, and instead of acknowledging that it wasn't an appropriate time for either of us to be together, I stupidly held the friendship hostage, as if I would ever be able to stop loving her just because it wasn't feasible to have affection or hang on one another's words for hour after countless hour every night. The stress of life caught up to her and caused her to break it off, and because the friendship was being used as a bargaining chip...

...let's just say the idea that I could ever choose to stop caring about someone is preposterous. Of course I still love her. And she was hot. And she was brilliant. But it wasn't the right time. TL;DR:
It can happen but don't force it. Especially if it's one-sided, DON'T FORCE IT. If it doesn't happen on its own, it may never, so don't hold your breath. And especially don't hold your breath about your feelings. Be open to working with them about how to manage it until you acclimate. Why? Because there are as many relationships as there are people. on the earth and all we can generalize on is the framework at the bottom; let the rest emerge as it shall, because that's what it will do whether we like it or not.
